title: Vaccinations
subtitle: About all the important vaccines and which ones are needed at different life stages.

sections.heading: 1. What a vaccine is and why it's needed
sections.body:
A vaccine is a veterinary product that trains the immune system to recognize and destroy viruses or bacteria without the animal developing the actual disease. There are several types of vaccines (live, inactivated, recombinant, and others).
It's important to understand: a vaccine doesn't treat a disease. It prepares the body in advance for an encounter with an infection.

sections.heading: 2. How a vaccine works
sections.body:
After a vaccine is administered, several stages take place.
1. The immune system meets the pathogen. The body recognizes that a “foreign” agent has appeared. Although the real virus doesn't cause disease (or may not even be present at all), the immune system reacts as if a real infection had occurred.
2. Antibody production begins. The body produces special proteins called antibodies. These are what can quickly recognize the real virus and neutralize it.
3. Memory cells form. This is the most important stage. The immune system remembers: what the virus looks like; how to destroy it quickly; which antibodies are needed specifically against it. This memory can last for several years, and sometimes almost a lifetime, depending on the disease.
4. When a real infection occurs, the immune system recognizes the virus almost instantly, antibodies are produced very quickly, and the virus doesn't have time to multiply much. As a result, three outcomes are possible: the cat doesn't get sick at all; the illness passes very mildly; the risk of death drops by tens of times.

sections.heading: 3. Why treatment can't replace vaccination
sections.body:
Many viral diseases in cats are practically untreatable. For example: panleukopenia; rabies; some forms of viral leukemia.
A veterinarian can only treat the consequences: dehydration; inflammation; secondary infections; seizures; breathing problems.
The body itself must defeat the virus on its own. If the immune system hasn't been trained in advance, the chances are significantly lower.

sections.heading: 4. Why immunity doesn't kick in right away
sections.body:
Building a full immune response takes time. The body usually needs 2 to 4 weeks after vaccination to produce enough antibodies and memory cells. During this period, the animal is still vulnerable.
Typically: the first antibodies appear after 5-7 days; solid protection forms after 2-4 weeks.

sections.heading: 5. Types of vaccines: core vaccines
sections.body:
All cat vaccines are conventionally divided into two large groups.
Core vaccines are recommended for all cats, regardless of age, breed, or lifestyle — even if the animal never goes outside. The reason is simple: pathogens can be brought into the home on shoes, clothing, hands, or objects.
1. Panleukopenia (Feline Panleukopenia Virus, FPV). The most dangerous viral disease in cats. Also known as feline distemper or infectious enteritis. It affects the intestines, bone marrow, and immune system. Mortality in kittens can reach 90%. The virus is very resistant and can survive in the environment for more than a year.
2. Feline herpesvirus (FHV-1). Causes viral rhinotracheitis. Main symptoms: runny nose, eye ulcers, conjunctivitis, sneezing, coughing, difficulty breathing. After recovery, the virus remains in the body for life, and the disease can return during periods of stress.
3. Calicivirus (FCV). A very common virus. Causes mouth ulcers, tongue inflammation, high fever, runny nose, lameness, and sometimes severe pneumonia. There are many strains of the virus, so a vaccinated cat can sometimes still get sick, but the illness is much milder.
4. Rabies. Almost always fatal once symptoms appear, and dangerous not only to animals but also to humans. In many countries the vaccine is required by law, especially if the cat travels, goes outdoors, participates in shows, or crosses national borders.

sections.heading: 6. Types of vaccines: non-core
sections.body:
These vaccines are given only when risk factors are present.
1) Feline leukemia (FeLV). A very serious viral disease. Affects the immune system, bone marrow, and blood. Increases the risk of tumors, severe infections, and anemia. The vaccine is recommended for kittens, cats with outdoor access, and animals that come into contact with other cats.
2) Chlamydiosis (Chlamydia felis). A bacterial infection causing severe conjunctivitis, eye discharge, and inflammation of the respiratory tract. Usually given in catteries, shelters, and homes with many cats.
3) Bordetella bronchiseptica. Causes upper respiratory infections, more common in shelters, boarding facilities, and catteries. Most house cats don't need this vaccine.
4) FIV (feline immunodeficiency virus). A vaccine exists in some countries, but it is used on a limited basis, doesn't provide full protection, and can complicate diagnosis of the disease.
5) FIP (feline infectious peritonitis). An intranasal vaccine against feline coronavirus exists, but its effectiveness is considered insufficiently proven.
For a cat that lives exclusively indoors, the following are usually recommended: panleukopenia, herpesvirus, calicivirus. Rabies — depending on legal requirements, travel, and your veterinarian's recommendations. FeLV usually isn't required if the cat doesn't have contact with other animals.

sections.heading: 7. Why kittens are vaccinated multiple times
sections.body:
This has to do with maternal antibodies. In the first weeks of life, a kitten receives protection through its mother's milk. These antibodies protect the kitten, but they also interfere with the vaccine's ability to work.
If vaccinated too early, maternal antibodies will destroy the vaccine. If vaccinated too late, maternal protection will already be gone while the kitten's own immunity isn't yet established.
That's why vaccination is given as a series: 8 weeks; 12 weeks; sometimes 16 weeks. This practically guarantees a moment when the vaccine can “teach” the immune system.

sections.heading: 8. What happens without revaccination
sections.body: Immune memory gradually weakens. Antibody levels decrease, and memory cells work less effectively. Over time, protection drops to the point where the body once again becomes susceptible to infection. This is why most vaccines require repeated doses.

sections.heading: 9. Can a vaccinated cat still get sick
sections.body: Yes, no vaccine offers a 100% guarantee. However, a vaccinated cat will go through the illness much more easily, without serious complications and with minimal risk to life. The goal of vaccination is to reduce the severity of disease and prevent fatal outcomes.

sections.heading: 10. Safety of modern vaccines
sections.body:
Modern vaccine products undergo strict quality control and are highly purified. Side effects are possible (lethargy, a slight fever), but they are rare and pass quickly.
The risk of severe complications after vaccination is a fraction of a percent. Meanwhile, the risk of death from certain infections reaches: 50-90% for panleukopenia; nearly 100% for rabies once symptoms appear. This is exactly why veterinary organizations around the world consider vaccination one of the most effective measures for protecting cats' health.

sections.heading: 11. How often vaccines need to be updated (revaccination)
sections.body:
Revaccination is the repeated administration of a vaccine after the initial vaccination, to maintain immune protection.
Primary kitten vaccination: 8-9 weeks — first vaccine against panleukopenia, herpesvirus, and calicivirus; 12 weeks — second dose; 16 weeks — a third dose may be needed if vaccination started early; 12-16 weeks — first rabies vaccine; 12 months after completing the primary course — first revaccination.
Adult cats: panleukopenia (FPV) — immunity lasts a long time, revaccinate every 3 years; herpesvirus (FHV-1) and calicivirus (FCV) — annually if risk is high, every 3 years if risk is low; rabies — the interval depends on the vaccine and national law (1 or 3 years); FeLV — annually if the risk of infection persists.

sections.heading: 12. Frequency for cats
sections.body:
Kittens: the highest risk of severe infections — vaccination is especially important.
Adult cats (1-7 years): with timely vaccination, immunity is usually well maintained.
Senior cats (over 10-12 years): age by itself isn't a reason to skip vaccination, but a clinical exam is done before the shot.
A veterinarian may recommend an individualized schedule if the cat: roams freely outdoors; lives in a cattery or shelter; travels frequently; has chronic illnesses; has an immune deficiency; is being treated with immunosuppressive drugs; is pregnant or nursing kittens.

sections.heading: 13. Do vaccines need to be given for life?
sections.body: In most cases — yes. Even though some vaccines are given only once every three years, regular revaccination remains an important part of prevention. Protection doesn't become “permanent” with age, so at every annual checkup the veterinarian assesses the cat's health, infection risk, and determines which vaccines truly need to be updated that year.

title: Introducing Two Cats in an Apartment
subtitle: Cat psychology and understanding the steps.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction to the problem of combining cats
sections.body:
The cohabitation of domestic cats and humans began roughly 10,000 years ago as a mutually beneficial arrangement: cats controlled rodent populations near fields and grain stores. Unlike most other domesticated animals, the domestication of cats didn't require major genetic changes — their innate behavior and hunting instincts remained almost untouched. The modern house cat largely retains the habits of its wild ancestor, the African wildcat, which evolved as a solitary hunter that defends its territory and avoids direct fights to prevent injury.
In today's urban environments, the overwhelming majority of cats live within the closed confines of an apartment. For the animals, this creates a serious conflict with their nature: limited space deprives them of their natural ways of controlling their territory and keeping distance from strangers.
In the practice of veterinarians who specialize in animal behavior, about a quarter of all cases involve conflicts between cats living in the same home. It's crucial to note that in most cases, the cause of a prolonged conflict is the improper introduction of a new cat into territory where a resident cat already lives.
Understanding how cats think, how their bodies respond to stress, and how they build relationships with one another is critical for a successful introduction. Mistakes made in the early stages lead to persistent behavioral problems (aggression, urinating outside the litter box) and serious physical illnesses that arise from ongoing nervous tension.

sections.heading: 2. The basics of cat behavior and social life
sections.body:
Contrary to the popular myth that cats always walk alone, they actually have a great deal of flexibility in how they socialize. Cats can indeed survive alone when food is scarce, but when resources are plentiful, they're capable of forming complex social groups — colonies.
The core of such a cat group is always based on maternal kinship: the heart of the colony is made up of mothers, daughters, and sisters. They band together to raise kittens, defend territory, and control food sources. Females in the group cooperate beautifully: they groom, guard, and even nurse each other's kittens. Thanks to this, kittens develop faster and become independent, on average, 10 days earlier than kittens raised by solitary mothers.
Within their group, cats choose their own “best friends”: they sleep pressed up against each other and regularly exchange friendly greetings. However, cat society isn't uniform: some animals may avoid each other, creating a complex web of likes and dislikes. In groups of unneutered animals, males tend to avoid each other more due to competition, but once the animals are neutered, sex no longer plays much of a role in choosing a friend. What matters most for good relationships is blood relation and whether the cats grew up together from a young age.

sections.heading: 3. Communication through scent and the concept of a “group scent”
sections.body:
Defending one's home from outsiders is a basic instinct. The appearance of an unfamiliar animal in the apartment always triggers anxiety and often aggression from the resident cat, because cats tell “their own” from “strangers” primarily by scent.
Cats living peacefully together constantly rub against one another with their sides, heads, and tails. During this pleasant ritual, they actively exchange pheromones and secretions from glands located on the face and between the paw pads. Together with constant mutual sniffing, this creates a unique “shared group scent,” which serves as their main signal of safety.
When a new cat with a completely foreign scent is brought into the home, the resident cat perceives this as an invasion and a direct threat to its home. Even if your own cat has just come back from a short trip to the vet smelling of medication, other cats in the household may fail to recognize it and attack.

sections.heading: 4. Differences in aggression between solitary cats and groups
sections.body:
How cats express aggression depends heavily on the number of animals in the household. If a cat lives alone, it's more likely to bite or scratch its owners — since humans are its only source of interaction and play, playful aggression or fear-based aggression gets redirected at people.
If several cats live in the home, the level of hidden tension is usually higher, and aggression is directed at other cats: flattened ears, hissing, loud yowling, blocking passageways, and trying to avoid each other's line of sight. The more cats there are, the higher the competition for food, litter boxes, and attention, which requires the owner to distribute the apartment's space very thoughtfully.
Criteria for choosing a second cat: how to reduce the risk of conflict. A successful introduction begins even before you bring the new pet home. Veterinary specialists strongly advise against getting a new pet if your first cat is already elderly or suffers from chronic illness — the stress of a noisy new competitor showing up can seriously worsen its health.
When choosing a new companion, consider: age and temperament (an adult cat does better with an animal of a similar temperament; kittens adapt more easily between 2-9 weeks of age); kinship and adopting in pairs (a brother and sister, or an already-bonded pair from a shelter, sharply reduce the risk of conflict — they already share a scent and an attachment); a trial period (foster-to-adopt) — many shelters offer temporary fostering so you can assess compatibility before making a final decision.
A failed introduction and a hidden territorial war take a severe toll on both animals' bodies. Hidden competition causes a state of chronic stress that damages health.

sections.heading: 5. Hormonal response and nervous system breakdown
sections.body:
When a cat senses a threat, its brain sends a signal to the systems that control stress (the hypothalamus, pituitary, and adrenal glands) and also activates the sympathetic nervous system. Normally, during a sudden fright, the adrenal glands release the hormone cortisol, giving the body a burst of energy to carry out the “fight or flight” instinct.
But if a cat is trapped in an apartment with a hostile housemate, it can't run away. The inability to escape the threat turns ordinary fear into toxic, unending stress. The nervous system stays constantly overstimulated, and the adrenal glands become depleted and stop responding normally. Studies of the brains of chronically stressed cats show major changes in the production of catecholamines, which are responsible for anxiety.
Hair analysis in cats (which can track cortisol levels over an extended period) shows that animals that never leave the apartment already have higher baseline stress levels than cats that go outside. A closed-in space by itself keeps a cat in a state of tension, and adding a rival to that environment often becomes the final straw that leads to illness and poor behavior.
Feline idiopathic cystitis (FIC) driven by nervous tension. A classic consequence of ongoing stress from territorial disputes is inflammation of the bladder — a complex condition caused by a malfunction in the central nervous system. The constant release of stress hormones makes the bladder walls too permeable, so caustic components of urine penetrate deeper into the tissue and irritate pain receptors. As a result, the cat often runs to the litter box, experiences significant pain, and blood may appear in the urine.
Most important of all: when a cat starts urinating on the owner's bed or rugs, this is a direct result of pain and anxiety — it's trying to leave its scent in the safest place available, one that smells like its beloved owner. This is in no way “revenge” against the new cat. In most animals, cystitis symptoms resolve on their own once the cats are reconciled with each other or the source of fear is removed.

sections.heading: 6. How to recognize conflict: signs of hidden aggression
sections.body:
Many owners think: “If the cats aren't fighting until there's blood and fur flying, they must have become friends.” In reality, cats prefer to settle disputes simply by avoiding each other. The absence of fights often masks deep hostility that shows up through passive aggression and resource control.
Resource control happens when one cat systematically blocks another from things essential to its life: high places (shelves, cat trees) — cats compete for these more fiercely than for food; litter boxes — using the litter box is a moment of maximum vulnerability, and if one cat stakes out another at the box, it's one of the most powerful forms of psychological pressure; narrow passageways — doorways, hallways, landings in front of stairs; social resources — human attention, the right to sit on a lap or sleep in the bed.
If you notice the warning signs in time, you can stop a conflict before claws come out. A typical scenario: one of the cats starts urinating outside the litter box even though it's perfectly healthy — meanwhile the other cat constantly lies in the hallway, cutting off the path to the box. Creating a separate “safe room” for the frightened animal helps.
A scale of signs (from less to more alarming): “The hard stare” — a fixed, unblinking look down at the opponent, a quiet form of passive aggression and an early sign of stress. Blocking pathways — deliberately lying in narrow passageways; the cat pretends to sleep, but a nervously twitching tail and radar-like ears give away that it's controlling territory — a sign of high hidden tension. Intercepting and looming — the aggressor quickly finishes its own food and then sits right up against the victim's bowl, forcing it to leave hungry, or constantly beats the victim to the owner — active resource control. Freezing — the intimidated cat freezes mid-step at the sight of the aggressor, presses itself to the floor, and tries to leave by another route — chronic fear. Time-sharing — the cats sleep in the same spots and use the same routes, but strictly at different times of day so they never cross paths — hidden avoidance. Open threats — hissing, loud guttural yowling, growling, ears flattened, pupils huge, fur standing on end — critical aggression, readiness to fight.

sections.heading: 7. Preparing the apartment: Five rules for a healthy feline environment
sections.body:
Before introducing the animals face to face, you need to properly prepare the apartment. International veterinary organizations have developed the “Five Pillars of a Healthy Feline Environment” — following them alone significantly reduces stress.
1. A safe hiding place for each cat. Every cat needs a place where it can hide from danger and calm down. An ideal hideaway is elevated, lets the cat stretch out to its full length, and has two exits (so no one can corner it).
2. Separating essential resources. The main mistake is putting all the bowls and litter boxes in a row in a single room. The rule of “number of cats + 1” should apply to litter boxes, bowls, and scratching posts: for two cats you need three litter boxes, spread across different rooms, so that one dominant cat can't control them all at once.
3. The chance to hunt and play. Playing with wand toys and food puzzles helps cats burn off pent-up energy and relieve nervous tension. Playing together also helps a great deal during the introduction process.
4. Positive interaction with people. The cat should always be the one to initiate contact. Never restrain a cat by force, and especially never grab it by the scruff. If the animal resists or is tense, leave it alone and don't pick it up.
5. Respect for scent. Avoid using household chemicals with strong smells, and take off outdoor shoes. Provide cats with comfortable scratching posts so they can leave their scent marks — this gives them a sense of confidence that the territory belongs to them.

sections.heading: 8. A scientific protocol for safe introductions
sections.body:
The old approach of “just put the newcomer in the room and let them sort out who's boss” is fundamentally wrong and dangerous: it causes a massive surge of stress hormones and often leads to cats becoming terrified of each other for years to come. The modern approach calls for a gradual, step-by-step introduction. The pace of this process is always set by whichever cat is more afraid.
Step 1: Isolation in “base camp.” A separate, closed-off room is set up for the new cat, with its own litter boxes, bowls, water, and scratching post. The door stays firmly closed, and the cats shouldn't see each other. The newcomer lowers its stress level after the move and leaves its scent while feeling safe, while the resident cat understands there's a stranger in the house but that its main territory remains secure.
Step 2: Scent swapping. The owner takes a clean cloth and gently strokes the cheeks and chin of the first cat with it (soothing pheromones are released there), then brings that cloth into the newcomer's room. If the cat calmly sniffs the unfamiliar scent, it's immediately given its favorite treat — the same thing is then done in the other direction. This builds pleasant associations: the strange, unfamiliar scent becomes linked with getting delicious food and stops feeling frightening.
Step 3: Swapping territories. Once both cats react calmly to the scented cloths, they're temporarily swapped — the newcomer is let out to explore the whole apartment, while the resident cat is shut in the newcomer's room for that time. This is a crucial stage for creating that shared, blended “group scent” that will bring peace.
Step 4: Controlled visual contact. A transparent barrier is placed between the animals (a tall baby gate, a screen, or a door propped open with a sturdy stop), and food is offered to both cats on either side of the barrier, with the bowls gradually moved closer to the gate. If even one cat tenses up, stops eating, or its pupils dilate, the bowls are immediately moved back.
Step 5: A supervised meeting with no barrier. If the cats eat and play calmly through the screen, the barrier can be removed for a very short time (5-15 minutes), surrounded by plenty of toys. The owner's main job is to separate the cats back into different rooms before they have a chance to hiss or fight. The length of these meetings is gradually increased until the animals are fully used to each other.

sections.heading: 9. What to do if a fight is brewing: the three-step rule
sections.body:
If something goes wrong and the cats show aggression, you need to act decisively:
1. Stop the conflict safely. Never try to separate fighting cats with your bare hands — in a state of full arousal they can bite you badly. Slide a piece of cardboard between them, or throw a thick blanket over them so they can no longer see each other.
2. Isolate. Immediately separate the cats that fought into different rooms and close the doors so they can calm down and their nervous systems can return to normal.
3. Solve the problem. Analyze why the breakdown happened: maybe you moved too fast, there aren't enough litter boxes, or the cats have nowhere to jump up to escape the conflict.
Using pheromones and calming aids. If the tension between the animals is very high, it's worth using special products that affect how cats perceive scent, or medication.

sections.heading: 10. Synthetic pheromones
sections.body:
There are two main types of cat pheromone products available for purchase.
The first type helps cats feel more confident in their territory (an analog of facial pheromones). It works well if a cat has started marking corners with urine due to stress, but it works poorly for reconciling two cats.
To resolve conflicts between cats living together, an analog of the Cat Appeasing Pheromone is used — in nature, a mother cat produces it while nursing kittens so they feel safe and don't fight among themselves. Clinical trials using special plug-in diffusers showed excellent results: over a month and a half of use, the frequency and intensity of cat conflicts dropped significantly; constant fleeing from a housemate decreased by almost half; the effect doesn't appear immediately, but around the 2nd-3rd week of use. Even after the diffusers were switched off following a month of use, the cats continued to live peacefully — the pheromone had helped them form new, good relationships that held up even without the product.

sections.heading: 11. The most common owner mistakes
sections.body:
Years of experience from veterinary behaviorists have produced a list of the main mistakes that most often ruin the introduction process:
1. “Let them sort it out themselves.” Cats don't live by a strict pack hierarchy the way dogs do. Forcing a face-to-face confrontation makes them retreat into rigid defensiveness rather than “figure out who's the boss.”
2. Punishing hissing. Never yell at a cat, hit it, or spray it with water for hissing at a newcomer. Hissing is a normal signal meaning “back off, I'm scared.” If you punish a cat for this warning, it will learn to attack silently and without warning, and the fear from the punishment will become linked to the presence of the other cat.
3. Feeding from two bowls placed right next to each other. If you put the bowls side by side, the cats will tolerate each other's presence for the sake of the food, but internally they'll experience tremendous stress and tension.
4. Ignoring illness. If your adult cat, previously friendly, suddenly becomes aggressive toward others, be sure to have its health checked by a vet. Hidden joint pain, worsening eyesight, or thyroid problems can make an animal very irritable — the cat takes out its physical pain on those around it and defends itself with aggression.

title: Behavior
subtitle: Body language, correcting unwanted habits, and games for feline happiness.
intro:
To understand the behavior of a house cat, you need to remember where it comes from.
Its ancestor is the African wildcat, a solitary territorial predator.

sections.heading: 1. Where cat habits come from: the past of a solitary hunter
sections.body:
To truly understand a house cat's reactions, you need to look into its past. Dogs descended from pack animals that know how to negotiate and make up after quarrels. But the ancestor of the domestic cat was the African wildcat — a committed loner. These predators lived alone, fiercely guarded their territory, and relied only on themselves. This history largely shapes the character of every cat today.
Even though cats have lived alongside humans for a long time, deep down they remain solitary hunters. However, they've turned out to be remarkably flexible: if there's plenty of food and the environment is calm, cats are quite capable of bonding both with other cats and with people.
A kitten learns to trust humans most easily during the so-called sensitive period — roughly from the second to the ninth week of life. But even the most affectionate cat needs, throughout its entire life, to feel that it's in control of the situation, understands what will happen next, and always has a way to retreat in case of danger.
Because cats have always lived alone, they never learned to display submission (the way dogs do to avoid a fight). When faced with a threat, a cat prefers to freeze, hide, or flee — it will only attack openly as an absolute last resort, when there's nowhere left to run. What's more, in the wild, showing pain or weakness is very dangerous — it makes you easy prey. Because of this instinct, cats are phenomenally good at hiding illness and severe pain, which often becomes a problem, since owners and even veterinarians don't always notice in time that an animal is unwell.

sections.heading: 2. Body language: how cats talk without words
sections.body:
Cats are constantly communicating with the world, just not the way we do. They rarely use their voice, relying instead on body language: postures, tail movements, facial expressions, and muscle tension. To understand a cat, you need to look at the whole picture — judging by just one detail (say, only the tail) can lead you badly astray.
Tail position is an excellent mood indicator. A tail held straight up says the cat is confident, friendly, and ready to interact; if the tip curls like a question mark, that's a warm greeting. A relaxed tail held at back level or slightly lower means the cat is calm but still keeping an eye on things. If a cat is scared or anxious, it tucks its tail between its hind legs, trying to make itself as small as possible. But when badly frightened or ready to defend itself, the reaction is the opposite: the fur on the tail stands on end and it puffs up like a bottle brush — the animal is trying to look bigger and more intimidating.
Tail movements matter just as much. If just the tip twitches slightly, the cat is intensely focused on something or hunting. But if the tail starts lashing sharply and forcefully from side to side, that's a clear sign the cat is angry or irritated, and the stronger and faster the tail whips, the closer the cat is to lunging at something. Conversely, if the tail wraps gently around your leg, that's the feline equivalent of a hug.
Cat ears can not only pick up the faintest sounds but also reveal the subtlest shades of mood. Ears pointed forward and slightly outward signal relaxed curiosity. If they drop and splay out to the sides (the “airplane” position), the cat is uncomfortable and anxious. Ears pressed flat against the head are a sign of serious fear or readiness to fight (this protects them from injury). If one ear points forward and the other points back, the cat is confused and trying to listen to several things at once.

sections.heading: 3. How to recognize hidden pain: the Feline Grimace Scale (FGS)
sections.body:
Since cats instinctively hide their illnesses, figuring out when they're in pain is very difficult. A cat in severe pain may not cry or meow at all — it may simply become listless and hide. To solve this problem, researchers at the University of Montreal developed a special scale (the Feline Grimace Scale, FGS) that lets you assess pain levels just from the animal's facial expression, with no complicated equipment needed.
This method is based on the fact that facial muscles contract reflexively in response to pain, and a cat can't control this. To assess a cat using this scale, you need to observe it for about 30 seconds while it's not sleeping, eating, or grooming. Five areas of the face are scored, each rated from 0 to 2 points, and the points are then added together. Studies have shown that a score of 4 or higher means the cat really is in significant pain and needs pain medication urgently.
It's important to remember that in flat-faced cats (Persians, for example), it's harder to judge tension in the muzzle and whiskers, but the eyes and ears will still give an accurate result.

sections.heading: 4. Joy, trust, and affection: how cats show it
sections.body:
Cats don't have as rich a range of facial expressions as we or monkeys do. They show their joy and love through scent, posture, and sound. If you learn to notice these signals, you'll understand just how much your pet loves you.
One of the clearest signs of complete trust is the “slow blink.” When a cat looks at you and slowly closes its eyes, it's essentially saying, “I'm not going to attack” (among predators, a direct, unblinking stare is a challenge). Researchers have found that if a person slowly blinks back while looking at a cat, the cat is likely to respond in kind — it's a great way to deliberately show a cat that you're friendly.
Another important sign is when a cat rubs its cheeks, chin, or head against you: it has special glands on its face that release calming pheromones. This isn't just about begging for food — this is how the cat marks you as “one of its own,” adds you to its family, and shows that you're safe to be around.
If a cat sleeps next to you, pressed against your body, it means it's entrusting you with its safety. The highest degree of trust is when a cat sleeps on its back, paws sprawled out, exposing its belly: in nature, the belly is the most vulnerable spot, and a cat will only expose it somewhere it doesn't expect any danger. And when a cat brings you its toys or a mouse it's caught, that's also an act of caring passed down from its wild ancestors: it's sharing its catch with you and trying to “feed” you.

sections.heading: 5. The secrets of purring: it's not just about pleasure
sections.body:
We tend to think that if a cat is purring, it must be perfectly happy. But science says it's much more complicated than that. Purring is produced by rhythmic contractions of the muscles in the larynx and diaphragm — scientists have even found special pads in cats' throats that can vibrate and generate this sound almost automatically as air passes through them.
Of course, cats purr when they feel good. But they've also learned to use purring to manipulate people. There's a so-called “solicitation” purr, which cats produce when asking for food or attention. Researchers found that hidden inside this sound is a high-pitched cry (at a frequency of 220-520 Hz) remarkably similar to a human infant's cry. Even people who've never owned a cat perceive this sound as urgent and distressing — it turns out cats have learned to exploit our parental instincts to get us to feed them faster.
But that's not all. Cats can also purr loudly when they're in severe pain, frightened, or giving birth. Some believe this is a form of self-healing: vibrations at purring frequencies (25 to 150 Hz) are thought to speed up wound healing, reduce inflammation, and even help broken bones knit faster.
In reality, it's important to remember that an animal may purr both out of joy, when hoping for a favorite treat, and in a state of high physiological stress.

sections.heading: 6. Stress and the Cat Stress Score (CSS)
sections.body:
Stress in cats is a serious problem that can be acute (short-term) or chronic (ongoing). While acute stress (being startled by a vacuum cleaner or a trip to the vet) simply mobilizes the body's resources, chronic stress slowly destroys a cat's health: at first the body tries to adapt, but eventually exhaustion sets in and the animal becomes seriously ill. To help shelter workers and veterinarians more easily gauge how stressed a cat is, the Cat Stress Score (CSS) was created, rating condition on a scale from 1 to 7.
Non-obvious causes of stress and “nerve-related” illness. Owners often have no idea what's making their cat constantly on edge. For instance, cats hear ultrasound extremely well, so rodent-repelling devices or the hum of household appliances can drive them up the wall. Strong smells also bother them a great deal — air fresheners or citrus essential oils, for example. And if a cat has no way to climb up high (onto a shelf or cat tree) to survey the room from above, it will constantly feel vulnerable.
Ongoing stress and elevated levels of cortisol (the “stress hormone”) lead to real illness. The most common problem is idiopathic cystitis: the bladder becomes painful and inflamed with no bacteria involved at all, purely from nerves, which can make the cat run to the litter box frequently or start urinating outside it. Many people think the cat is “getting revenge,” but really it's just sick. Cats may also start licking themselves until large bald patches form, trying to self-soothe. And if stress causes a cat to stop eating, that's extremely dangerous: starvation in cats can very quickly (within just a few days) lead to a fatal liver disease.

sections.heading: 7. The main mistakes owners make when interacting with cats
sections.body:
Because cats and humans perceive the world differently, our good intentions sometimes come across as frightening to them. Understanding these differences will help you live in harmony with your pet.
Petting mistakes: why a cat suddenly bites. The biggest mistake is assuming that if a cat rolls onto its back and shows its belly, it's asking for a belly rub. An exposed belly is a sign that the cat trusts you, but if you start petting it, the predator's instinct kicks in: the belly must be protected! The nerve endings there are extremely sensitive, so the cat immediately reaches for claws and teeth — not out of spite, but simply as an ancient self-preservation reflex.
The second common mistake is petting a cat too long and too firmly along its whole back, especially toward the tail. This area is packed with nerve endings. If you pet it for too long, the cat's nervous system becomes overloaded and it starts to feel unpleasant. The result is “petting-induced aggression”: a moment ago the cat was purring, and now it's biting your hand just to make you stop.
You should pet a cat the way cats groom each other as a sign of friendship.

sections.heading: 8. Misunderstandings about behavior
sections.body:
In many movies and cartoons, a cat with an arched back is a symbol of aggression and evil. But in real life, it all depends on the situation. If a cat arches its back while approaching you, with relaxed muscles and ears pointed forward, it's simply having a nice stretch and saying hello. But if that same posture comes with fur standing on end, stiff legs, and flattened ears, the cat is panicking and trying to look bigger to defend itself from an attack. If you try to pet it to “calm it down,” it will fight for its life and attack.
Another amusing misunderstanding has to do with scent. Often a cat will sniff something new (your shoes, say) and then freeze with its mouth slightly open and a somewhat dazed look. People tend to think the cat is expressing disgust. In fact, behind the front teeth on the roof of a cat's mouth is a special structure called the vomeronasal (Jacobson's) organ — an extra nose for analyzing the most complex scents and pheromones. By opening its mouth slightly, the cat directs scent molecules straight to it — so it's not wrinkling its face in disgust, it's thoughtfully and deeply analyzing the smell.

sections.heading: 9. Don't force interaction, and respect personal boundaries
sections.body:
The world's leading veterinary organizations insist that the single most important thing for a cat's mental well-being is a sense of control. The most serious mistake owners can make is forcibly dragging a frightened cat out from under the couch or holding it in their arms while it struggles to get free. For a cat, which is a loner by nature, any loss of freedom feels, on an emotional level, like it's about to be killed.
If a cat is getting used to a new home, or is simply frightened (guests arriving, for example), always give it the chance to hide somewhere safe, ideally elevated off the floor.
And the golden rule: the cat should always be the one to initiate affection and play. Never force your company on it.

sections.heading: 1. Hormones and the feline reproductive cycle
sections.body:
A cat's reproductive cycle depends on the season and the amount of daylight. In the Northern Hemisphere, cats are most active in spring and summer, when days are long. From October to December comes a resting period — anestrus — when sex hormone (estrogen) levels drop to a minimum. However, in cats living indoors under artificial lighting (around 14 hours of light per day), this cycle can run year-round regardless of season.
A cat's cycle consists of several stages, each with its own hormones, behaviors, and physical changes.
Proestrus (preparation for heat) lasts a very short time, usually less than a day: the body begins producing estrogen in preparation for possible mating. The cat becomes very affectionate and rubs against objects, but doesn't yet allow males near her.
Estrus (heat itself) is the period when the cat is ready to mate. It lasts from 2 to 19 days (about a week on average). Eggs mature in the ovaries and hormone levels rise sharply, which changes the cat's behavior: she adopts a distinctive posture (arching her back and holding her tail to the side), meows loudly, rolls on the floor, and eats less. Owners who haven't seen this before sometimes think the cat is sick or in pain.
Veterinary medicine also recognizes other variations of heat: “split heat” — when signs begin, fade for a couple of days, and then return again (common in young cats); prolonged heat — when heat lasts longer than a week (common in Siamese cats), which can be linked to hormonal cysts on the ovaries.
If fertilization doesn't occur, interestrus (the interval between heat cycles) follows, lasting about a week — hormone levels drop, but new follicles immediately begin maturing, so the lull doesn't last long and the exhausting cycle starts all over again.

sections.heading: 2. The mystery of ovulation: what triggers it
sections.body:
For a long time it was believed that cats could only become pregnant as a result of mechanical stimulation during mating — this is triggered by microscopic barbs on the male cat's penis, which set off the necessary nerve reflex.
However, modern research has shown that in more than 30% of cats, ovulation can occur spontaneously — without any male involvement at all. This process can be triggered by the scent of a male, the presence of other cats in heat nearby, or even simply a person petting the cat's back and lower back.
The main problem with spontaneous ovulation is that if the cat doesn't become pregnant, her body still begins preparing for motherhood (a false pregnancy sets in, lasting up to 50 days). During this time the uterus is exposed for a prolonged period to the hormone progesterone — this protects against new heat cycles but significantly raises the risk of serious infections and uterine cysts.
Pregnancy in cats lasts about two months (65-66 days on average). Labor itself takes anywhere from 4 to 42 hours. Cats are very fertile: a litter usually contains 1 to 5 kittens, and the probability of becoming pregnant after mating is very high — almost 74%.

sections.heading: 3. The male reproductive system
sections.body:
For a population to grow this quickly, male cats need to be active too. Sexual maturity in male cats comes with rising testosterone, which is what causes those barbs to develop on the penis, stimulating the female.
Veterinarians advise not allowing male cats to breed before they reach one year of age, so their bodies are fully developed and their sperm is of good quality. Male cats' reproductive capability lasts until 10-12 years of age, though semen quality declines with age.
If a male cat is infertile or has health problems, mating still triggers ovulation in the female, but pregnancy doesn't occur — as a result, the female suffers from a false pregnancy, and her risk of uterine disease increases. In addition, unneutered male cats often mark territory, are aggressive toward other animals, and need to be kept isolated.

sections.heading: 4. How the population grows: facts and myths
sections.body:
There are a lot of myths surrounding cat reproduction. The most famous is the legend that a single pair of cats and their descendants can produce 420,000 kittens in just 7 years. In practice, this figure is impossible, since it assumes ideal conditions: 100% survival of every kitten, immediate maturation, and no disease or aging. If biological laws really worked that perfectly, a single city would produce 76 billion cats in 10 years.
Realistic scientific calculations account for the high mortality rate on the streets: about 75% of stray kittens die within their first few months of life from infection, parasites, starvation, and vehicles. Factoring in this harsh reality, a pair of cats and their descendants over 7 years produce a much smaller, but still alarming, number — around 100 animals.
Modern computer models help calculate exactly how a population grows and how spaying/neutering affects it. If no measures are taken in a closed colony of 50 cats, roughly 1,000 kittens will be born and die from the hardships of life there over 10 years. Modeling shows that simple trapping and euthanasia don't work nearly as effectively as mass sterilization (TNR programs: Trap-Neuter-Return). Once the sterilization rate reaches the necessary threshold, the number of new kittens drops to zero, the population stabilizes, and then begins to decline.

sections.heading: 5. The health and longevity benefits of spaying/neutering
sections.body:
Spaying/neutering doesn't just address the problem of homeless animals — it also protects the health of an individual pet. Large-scale medical studies show that neutered male cats live, on average, 62% longer than intact males, and spayed females live 39% longer than unspayed ones. This gap has a simple explanation: neutered animals are less likely to roam away from home, don't get into street fights (and therefore don't contract dangerous viruses like FIV or leukemia), and don't develop diseases of the reproductive system.
Pyometra (a pus-filled infection of the uterus) is a life-threatening condition in which the uterus fills with pus. It used to be thought that only dogs suffered from it, but cats are affected just as much, especially in middle and older age (around 7.5 years on average). The disease develops because of hormones: repeated false pregnancies cause the uterine lining to thicken and secrete large amounts of fluid, while local immunity drops, letting bacteria (often E. coli) easily get inside. Symptoms in cats are often hidden — discharge isn't always noticed, since cats are very meticulous about grooming themselves — instead, the animal becomes lethargic, refuses food, and may vomit. The main treatment is emergency surgery to remove the uterus and ovaries; if delayed, blood poisoning (sepsis) can set in. Routine, planned spaying completely eliminates the risk of this disease.
Mammary gland tumors are the third most common cancer in cats. Unlike in dogs, where about half of such tumors are benign, more than 90% of these growths in cats are malignant, growing very quickly and spreading to the lungs. The main driver of these tumors' growth is sex hormones released during heat cycles, so the best prevention is spaying at the right time.
Based on this evidence, veterinary organizations around the world have launched the “Fix by Five” campaign: it's recommended that kittens have their planned surgery strictly before they turn 5 months old. Myths claiming that early spaying/neutering harms growth or somehow narrows the urethra in male cats have long been disproven by science — surgery at a young age is much easier for animals to recover from, they wake from anesthesia faster, and shelters stop filling up with unwanted kittens.
